speakers: Andrew Beer (Dynamic Beta Investments, manager of DBMF replication ETF)
summary: Weekly systematic-investor episode, April 2026: CTA/trend performance during the Iran-conflict March reversal, then Beer argues simple, efficient replication of the SG CTA index beats complex hedge-fund models because of implementation costs, and that bank QIS trend products lose most of their backtest Sharpe live.

coverage.note: trend barometer, CTA index returns, speed of models
Q1 CTA performance, Jan-Feb trend, March reversal, energy
CTA ETF vs mutual fund vs hedge fund complexity and returns
selection bias, early contrarian trades, signal vs implementation
quant on quant, capacity, cost of buying alpha
index composition bias, probability of beating index
data sources, index autocorrelation, active vs passive
trend not a definable beta, QIS growth
QIS underperformance and dispersion, index immutability
swap wrappers, tax and reported fees

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we've opened a Pandora's box that we don't really know what what what the parameters are
claims.claim: Geopolitical shock with unknowable parameters (9/11-style tail event) is a major unhedgeable risk in the current environment, argued by analogy to 9/11.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: All of those more or less could be fixed by the Federal Reserve coming in with a big bazooka
claims.claim: Earlier crises (GFC, pandemic) were fixed by Fed or fiscal action, but this ideology-driven geopolitical crisis cannot be, so it is a different regime that will persist.
claims.conditions: crisis driven by ideology rather than liquidity/credit

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the range of outcomes is not like between you know four and six
claims.claim: Geopolitical negotiation outcomes range from zero to ten, so markets whipsaw as they try to price each headline.
claims.conditions: binary-like geopolitical headline risk

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: in a war, the other side has a vote
claims.claim: Escalation by a transactional negotiator lets the counterparty choose when to de-escalate, so unintended consequences and large two-sided jumps are possible.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they're basically giving us for like $20 a month
claims.claim: AI tools that cost hundreds of billions to build are cheap to use, giving asset managers large efficiency gains in programming and trade reconciliation rather than in the investment strategy itself.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own trend barometer yesterday uh closed at 48 which indicates kind of a neutral environment right now
claims.claim: A trend barometer reading near 48 signals a neutral, directionless trend environment where markets flip day to day on Middle East headlines.
claims.testable: partly - proprietary gauge, definition not given

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: being slow has certainly in these situations been useful
claims.claim: In whipsaw regimes of the last three years, slower trend models have fared better than faster ones, although speed may differentiate returns differently this time.
claims.direction: slow models better in choppy markets
claims.conditions: headline-driven reversals; last three years only
claims.testable: yes - compare fast vs slow trend indices

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the Btop 50 index was up 83 basis points
claims.claim: Reported YTD index returns: BTOP50 above 8%, SG CTA about 8.5%, SG Trend about 8.5%, short-term traders 4.78% (as of a Tuesday in April 2026), showing CTAs positive despite the neutral trend environment.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short-Term Traders indices

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think that's a great testament really to how risk management um and how people are are um really focused on on this
claims.claim: On a day when markets moved against CTA positioning, CTA returns were only slightly negative, which Niels attributes to risk management discipline.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: that should be one of those iconic quarters that you point to when it the strategy is really doing doing its job
claims.claim: Q1 2026 SG CTA +7.5% while US equities fell and bonds were flat or down is an example of the crisis-alpha role of trend following, though one quarter is not a year.
claims.indicator: SG CTA index vs S&P 500 and bonds
claims.direction: long CTAs as diversifier in equity drawdown
claims.conditions: equity decline with flat/down bonds

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I've called it the the the great macro doover of 2026
claims.claim: Positions that worked in Jan-Feb (gold up 30%, non-US and EM equities) reversed violently in March when oil spiked, hitting funds that had been winning most.
claims.indicator: gold, non-US equities, EM equities, crude oil
claims.direction: trend positions reversed
claims.conditions: geopolitical oil shock after strong two-month trends

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: what we've seen in our portfolios is basically a gradual derisking
claims.claim: The replication model had no energy exposure at end-2025, added it from January as trends emerged, took a hit in March, and gradually de-risked positions that stopped working, including equity risk.
claims.direction: add energy exposure as trend forms; cut positions not working

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we've put on shinuards and knee pads maybe elbow pads
claims.claim: Rather than full crash-protection mode, the manager partially de-risks (shin guards and pads) when positions reverse in an unstable market.
claims.direction: partial de-risk
claims.conditions: unstable, headline-driven market

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: short-term models may have been a saving grace in March you know you may have gotten out faster
claims.claim: Either short-term models that exit quickly or broad diversification across many contracts (not concentrated in WTI) may explain which CTAs fared better in March.
claims.direction: short-term trend or wide diversification reduced March losses
claims.conditions: sharp reversal after escalation/de-escalation
claims.testable: yes - compare fast vs diversified CTA returns

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it plays out through through stocks and bonds at the same time which again have the same risk which is inflation
claims.claim: If the conflict raises inflation so stocks and bonds fall together as in 2022, trend following would again deliver a very strong year; if the world normalizes it lags equities.
claims.direction: long trend following when stocks and bonds fall together
claims.conditions: inflationary shock hitting both stocks and bonds
claims.testable: yes - 2022 analog and stock-bond correlation regimes

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: longerterm managers are overall still long even though with smaller positions
claims.claim: Longer-term trend managers remained long equities with reduced size, so the April equity rebound probably helped them, with currencies and precious metals also contributing.
claims.direction: long equities (smaller)
claims.conditions: April 2026 rebound

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the better you're doing in January, February, the more you got shellocked generally in in in March
claims.claim: In March 2026 the funds that did best in Jan-Feb lost the most, so CTA drawdown reflected crowded smart-money positioning across hedge funds, not a CTA-specific failure as in the Liberation Day episode.
claims.direction: winners of prior months were hit hardest
claims.conditions: common smart-money trades reverse together

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: Brevin Howard was down six
claims.claim: Named March 2026 returns: Citadel fixed income about -8%, Brevan Howard -6%, Capstone -15%, Marshall Wace Eureka -5%, plus wide dispersion among UCITS CTAs, supporting the crowding explanation.
claims.indicator: Bloomberg hedge fund return rankings (Nishant Kumar)

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: when people have done ETFs, they've tended to strip out a lot of complexity
claims.claim: The CTA product universe (hedge funds, then mutual funds and UCITS, then ETFs) falls in complexity, with ETFs simplified to plain trend with fewer instruments.
claims.testable: yes - classify products by instrument count

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: which is 40 basis points higher on an edify basis than the socken CTA index
claims.claim: Over the last five years the average CTA ETF returned about 6.1% a year with a higher Sharpe ratio than the SG CTA index and outperformed mutual funds and UCITS, so more complexity does not produce higher alpha.
claims.indicator: average CTA ETF vs SG CTA index, Morningstar data
claims.direction: simple/efficient CTA products outperform complex ones
claims.conditions: only five years of reliable data, 16 ETFs

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: this could all be selection bias a handful of funds happen to have launched
claims.claim: ETF outperformance may be selection bias from a few funds launching and doing well; Beer says the evidence has not yet shown that and will re-check periodically.
claims.testable: yes - re-test as the sample grows

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you can be early contrarian and right into a handful of big trades
claims.claim: Trend signals pay by catching a few big moves early, e.g. shorting Treasuries in Sept 2020 once yields rose from 0.5% to 0.7%, buying gold below 3,000 after a decade of failure, shorting crude at 105-110 and riding it down.
claims.direction: short Treasuries 2020, long gold, short crude
claims.conditions: large persistent trends from a modest initial signal
claims.testable: yes - trend backtests on these markets

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: not you know P&L from 100 different orthogonal positions
claims.claim: Most dollars made in CTAs come from a handful of big cross-asset trades, not from many orthogonal positions, so replication focuses on clusters and cross-asset relationships.
claims.direction: concentrate on clusters of related markets
claims.testable: yes - decompose CTA P&L by position

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: should I be long 15 different equity markets or should I compress that into a long EHA contract or a long EM contract
claims.claim: Use a complex model to detect the signal but a second decision (e.g. PCA/clustering) to implement it in fewer, more liquid contracts, such as one contract for global equity exposure.
claims.direction: compress many correlated markets into one liquid contract
claims.testable: yes - compare full vs compressed portfolios net of cost

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: quant on top of quant
claims.claim: Replication still needs complex underlying managers to produce the returns it replicates; complexity must exist somewhere even if the investor does not pay for it.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it works with $3 million, right? But it doesn't work with 50
claims.claim: Intraday or high-frequency trend models may show very high Sharpe but only at tiny capacity, so signal quality must be weighed against implementation capacity.
claims.conditions: fails as assets scale from 3 million to 50 to 500 million

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: let's get 300 basis points of excess returns on this thing but it's going to cost me 300 basis points
claims.claim: Gross excess return is worthless if the cost to implement it, including conditional liquidity, equals the gain; signal and implementation must be evaluated together.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: Yes, you need complexity for the signal.
claims.claim: Equity-index signals from many markets can be aggregated and implemented in fewer positions, so signal complexity does not require implementation complexity.
claims.testable: yes - test aggregation vs many-market implementation

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: We have outperformed every single one on an absolute and riskadjusted basis.
claims.claim: The replication model launched July 2016 outperformed each of the 20 SG CTA index constituents of that time on absolute and risk-adjusted return, supporting efficiency over complexity.
claims.indicator: replication model vs SG CTA constituents
claims.conditions: constituents as of 2016; later-added managers excluded

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: We've outperformed the overall the average by 400 basis points a year.
claims.claim: Claimed excess return of 400 bp a year over the average SG CTA index constituent since July 2016.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: what are the true implementation costs
claims.claim: True implementation costs (bid-ask, market impact in thin markets such as Chinese power or South African soybeans) are the unspoken problem of CTAs; quants are the dumb money that physical traders like Louis Dreyfus and Glencore pick off.
claims.direction: costs high in illiquid markets
claims.conditions: thin supply-demand markets with informed physical traders
claims.testable: partly - hard to observe impact cost

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: your execution price was slightly below where it ended for the day. But you're driving it.
claims.claim: A complex model trading a lot moves prices; when several similar managers trade together the price overshoots and then reverts, so execution looks fine against the close but adds hidden cost.
claims.conditions: many managers trading the same signal at the same time

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's a coin toss as to whether that market is going to trend enough
claims.claim: Implementation costs rise geometrically with the number of positions, so by position 180 or 350 the marginal market is a coin toss on whether it trends enough to pay for its costs.
claims.direction: fewer markets, more efficient
claims.conditions: disputed; some smart managers report hundreds of markets work
claims.testable: yes - marginal-market contribution net of cost

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: not a believer that trading hundreds of markets is necessarily better
claims.claim: Niels also doubts that trading hundreds of markets is better, though some peers do well with hundreds of markets due to exposure to different factors.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they get included in the index and so they're in the index today
claims.claim: Comparison to constituents of a fixed starting set is biased because later managers that did better were added to the index, so index composition changes over time (survivorship/inclusion).
claims.conditions: when comparing replication with a historical constituent list

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: The way for me to beat the index over time was to capture the signal more efficiently.
claims.claim: Beer could not beat the SG CTA index via own models, QIS products or manager selection, so he sought a structural efficiency advantage in capturing the same signal.
claims.testable: yes - replication tracking and excess return

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if you have a 54% chance probability you just keep doing it again and again and again
claims.claim: The replication beats the index in 54% of one-week rolling windows (overshoot +73 bp, undershoot -70 bp), which compounds to about 80% over a year and 90%+ over three years.
claims.conditions: no strong skew; small edge repeated often

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: 5 years, 10 years of data doesn't say much about the future
claims.claim: Five to ten years of performance data is limited evidence about the future of a product.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: I actually think the cleanest data on the space overall from a signal perspective is a multi-manager mutual fund in the US
claims.claim: Hedge funds cannot easily stop publishing; mutual fund and UCITS disclosure forces data, and a US multi-manager CTA mutual fund is the cleanest signal source.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: a lot of European managers have already closed their books
claims.claim: The SG CTA index has lagged autocorrelation because European managers close before US afternoon moves, making the replication signal foggier.
claims.conditions: US-hour market moves after Europe close
claims.testable: yes - test autocorrelation of index returns

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: An S&P 500 three basis point S&P 500 ETF is simply a better investment than trying to pick long only managers
claims.claim: Passive beating active is mathematically settled, yet active still has more assets, so product choice reflects behavior and distribution, not only cost.
claims.direction: passive low-cost over active

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: fund selectors are not rational value maximizer, sharp ratio maximizers
claims.claim: Fund selectors optimize for defensible choices (e.g. AQR with its 70-page papers) rather than Sharpe, so career risk shapes allocation flows.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's now 31% of the mutual funded ETF business in the US
claims.claim: Active ETFs are now 31% of the US mutual fund plus ETF business as mutual funds shrink, supporting wrapper migration.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you and I and all these people have different trend models or pick different QIS products and you're 20 points off
claims.claim: Trend following is not an identifiable beta: different trend models or QIS products can differ by 20-30 points, unlike US large-cap equity indices.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: by the time we specify all the different parameters
claims.claim: Merger arbitrage replication also fails as a single beta: once parameters are specified, portfolios concentrate in different deals and diverge.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the space really took off in I would say 2012 2013
claims.claim: Bank QIS products took off in 2012-13 after hedge funds embarrassed themselves in the GFC; allocators wanted cheaper, more liquid exposure.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: What's your sharp ratio live? 02.
claims.claim: Bank QIS products sold with long track records (e.g. G10 carry Sharpe 1.4 in backtest) show Sharpe near 0.2 live, as the track record is mostly a backtest.
claims.direction: backtest Sharpe overstated
claims.conditions: index launched with back-filled history
claims.testable: yes - compare backtest to live Sharpe

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: sorry, that one's gone. We have a new G10 currency thing.
claims.claim: QIS products are closed and replaced, so failing strategies disappear and surviving ones look better; this survivorship makes allocators unable to evaluate them.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: usually it's just made up stuff
claims.claim: Index backtests are what the bank wishes it had traded, with dials tuned, so they are weak evidence of future results.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: has done 200 basis points of excess returns less than the sog CTA index
claims.claim: About 17 tracked QIS trend products have returned roughly 200 bp a year less than the SG CTA index.
claims.indicator: 17 QIS trend products on Bloomberg vs SG CTA index

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the drop from the insample sharp ratio to the out of sample sharp ratio is 90%
claims.claim: QIS trend products lose about 90% of their Sharpe ratio between in-sample backtest and out-of-sample live.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you're basically get exposure to trend from banks for zero fees
claims.claim: Swap-based QIS trend products report no fees and can be layered as portable alpha, making them a bigger competitor to hedge funds than replication is.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it's a constant series of launching new indices
claims.claim: Indices are not supposed to change after launch, so banks launch new indices for each enhancement, producing a constant stream of products without live history.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: meaningfully more tax efficient than any other product out there
claims.claim: A swap-based ETF on an index can be 35 bp reported and more tax efficient, because derivatives allow a cheaper and tax-advantaged structure.
claims.direction: swap/derivative wrapper

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: 170 basis point mutual funds out there that probably have 200 basis points in trading costs
claims.claim: Reported fee comparisons ignore swap and trading costs; DBMF at 85 bp with near-zero trading cost competes against 170 bp mutual funds with about 200 bp trading costs.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: that's a negative trading cost because I'm comparing my execution price to the settlement price at the end of the day
claims.claim: UCITS fund transaction-cost calculations measure execution versus settlement, so pushing the price up while buying shows a negative cost, and some funds report zero costs when real costs are a couple of hundred bp.
claims.conditions: benchmark is end-of-day settlement price
claims.testable: yes - implementation shortfall vs arrival price

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: an investor might save 150 basis points
claims.claim: Tax efficiency (futures held in the entity, not Cayman subs; swap structure) could save about 150 bp a year in after-tax returns.
claims.direction: tax-efficient wrapper

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: easy for that person to make this a three or a 5% allocation
claims.claim: Model-portfolio allocators with 25 bp expense ratios need a low-cost, tax-efficient, ETF-style trend allocation sized at 3-5%.
claims.direction: 3-5% diversifier allocation
